Septic Arthritis: Kocher Criteria, Synovial Fluid Analysis, Diagnosis and Treatment

Definition

  • Joint infection by microorganisms
  • Mostly affect children less than 3 years old
  • Bacteria are the most significant pathogen because of their rapidly destructive nature
  • Non gonococcal and gonococcal bacterial septic arthritis
  • Non gonococcal: very aggressive. Staphylococcal infection (mostly S. aureus); Group A strep (strep pyogenes)
  • Gonococcal: caused by Neisseria gonorrhea. Most common 75% of cases of septic arthritis

Presentation

  • Progressive swelling of joint
  • Overlying skin of joint is warm and erythematous
  • Single joint but sometimes more than one is involved especially in neonates and younger children
  • Most commonly affected joints: hip, knee, ankle, elbow, wrist, shoulder
  • The joint is extremely tender
  • Patient unwilling to move their joint, the joint is held in position of most comfort, usually slight flexion
  • Onset is insidious and rapid
  • Systemic symptoms like fever, weakness, and headache

Attention!

  • Don’t overlook septic arthritis in joints that already have gout or rheumatoid arthritis
  • Sometimes the patient can move their joint because they already took steroids and analgesics over the counter which mask the inability to move
  • Sometimes the signs of septic joint is masked by antibiotics
  • IV drug abusers may have involvement of uncommon joints of the axial skeleton (eg sacroiliac, vertebral, sternoclavicular joints)

Diagnosis

If you suspect septic arthritis then:

  • Order FBC, ESR, CRP
  • Blood cultures, throat cultures
  • Joint aspiration is definitive but maybe delayed while waiting for laboratory studies
  • X ray may be initially normal or show only soft tissue swelling with displacement of capsular fat planes, later, features of bone destruction

Synovial fluid analysis

  • Normal / Septic arthritis
  • Color: Transparent / Yellow
  • Appearance: Clear / Purulent, turbid
  • WBC: < 1000 / > 50000
  • PMN: < 25% / > 75%
  • Special tests/crystals: Normal string sign / Gram stain, culture

Kocher criteria

  • Four criteria’s
  • Unable to weight bear the affected side — 1 point
  • ESR > 40 — 1 point
  • Fever > 38.5 C — 1 point
  • WBC > 12000 — 1 point
  • 1 point: 3%; 2 points: 40%; 3 points: 93%; 4 points: 99%

Types of microorganisms

  • Think gonococcal if: arthritis is migratory, monoarticular; patient is young and sexually active; slower onset of symptoms over several days; patient have symptoms of genital infection
  • If you don’t find purulent synovial fluid aspirate then you look for the triad (periarthritis, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgia)
  • Rash seen in Neisseria species in general
  • Think non gonococcal if: Aspiration of joint fluid reveal large number of WBCs and gram stain and cultures positive

Treatment

  • IV antibiotics
  • Staphylococcus species: IV vancomycin or IV clindamycin
  • When staphylococcus infect prosthetic joint then rifampin is added to the above
  • N gonorrhea: IV ceftriaxone followed by oral cefixime
  • Refer to orthopedic team for joint irrigation/drainage especially if non gonococcal
  • Analgesia
  • Splintage of the joint
